segs.e: Linked Discourses 21.1
1. Monks
With Kolita
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tatra kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhikkhū āmantesi:
segs.e: There Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the mendicants:
“Reverends, mendicants!”

segs.p: “Āvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa paccassosuṁ.
segs.e: “Reverend,” they replied.
Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this:

segs.p: “idha mayhaṁ, āvuso, rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
segs.e: “Just now, reverends, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind:
‘They speak of this thing called “noble silence”.
What then is this noble silence?’
It occurred to me:

segs.p: ‘idha bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṁ vūpasamā ajjhattaṁ sampasādanaṁ cetaso ekodibhāvaṁ avitakkaṁ avicāraṁ samādhijaṁ pītisukhaṁ dutiyaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: ‘As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.
This is called noble silence.’

segs.p: So khvāhaṁ, āvuso, vitakkavicārānaṁ vūpasamā ajjhattaṁ sampasādanaṁ cetaso ekodibhāvaṁ avitakkaṁ avicāraṁ samādhijaṁ pītisukhaṁ dutiyaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja vihariṁ.
segs.e: And so, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, I was entering and remaining in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

segs.p: Tassa mayhaṁ, āvuso, iminā vihārena viharato vitakkasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti.
segs.e: While I was in that meditation, perception and focus accompanied by placing the mind beset me.

segs.p: Atha kho maṁ, āvuso, bhagavā iddhiyā upasaṅkamitvā etadavoca:
segs.e: Then the Buddha came up to me with his psychic power and said,

segs.p: ‘moggallāna moggallāna, mā, brāhmaṇa, ariyaṁ tuṇhībhāvaṁ pamādo, ariye tuṇhībhāve cittaṁ saṇṭhapehi, ariye tuṇhībhāve cittaṁ ekodibhāvaṁ karohi, ariye tuṇhībhāve cittaṁ samādahā’ti.
segs.e: ‘Moggallāna, Moggallāna! Don’t neglect noble silence, brahmin! Settle your mind in noble silence; unify your mind and bring it to immersion in noble silence.’

segs.p: So khvāhaṁ, āvuso, aparena samayena vitakkavicārānaṁ vūpasamā ajjhattaṁ sampasādanaṁ cetaso ekodibhāvaṁ avitakkaṁ avicāraṁ samādhijaṁ pītisukhaṁ dutiyaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharāmi.
segs.e: And so, after some time, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, I entered and remained in the second absorption …

segs.p: Yañhi taṁ, āvuso, sammā vadamāno vadeyya:
segs.e: So if anyone should be rightly called

segs.p: ‘satthārā anuggahito sāvako mahābhiññataṁ patto’ti, mamaṁ taṁ sammā vadamāno vadeyya:
segs.e: a disciple who attained to great direct knowledge with help from the Teacher, it’s me.”
Linked Discourses 21.2
1. Monks
With Upatissa
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Tatra kho āyasmā sāriputto bhikkhū āmantesi:
segs.e: There Sāriputta addressed the mendicants:
“Reverends, mendicants!”

segs.p: “Āvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa paccassosuṁ.
segs.e: “Reverend,” they replied.
Sāriputta said this:

segs.p: “Idha mayhaṁ, āvuso, rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
segs.e: “Just now, reverends, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind:

segs.p: ‘atthi nu kho taṁ kiñci lokasmiṁ yassa me vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjeyyuṁ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā’ti?
segs.e: ‘Is there anything in the world whose decay and perishing would give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress in me?’
It occurred to me:

segs.p: ‘natthi kho taṁ kiñci lokasmiṁ yassa me vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjeyyuṁ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā’”ti.
segs.e: ‘There is nothing in the world whose decay and perishing would give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress in me.’”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, āyasmā ānando āyasmantaṁ sāriputtaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to him,

segs.p: “satthupi kho te, āvuso sāriputta, vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā nuppajjeyyuṁ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti?
segs.e: “Even if the Teacher were to decay and perish? Wouldn’t that give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress in you?”

segs.p: “Satthupi kho me, āvuso, vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā nuppajjeyyuṁ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā, api ca me evamassa:
segs.e: “Even if the Teacher were to decay and perish, that wouldn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress in me. Still, I would think:

segs.p: ‘mahesakkho vata bho satthā antarahito mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo.
segs.e: ‘Oh lord, the illustrious Teacher, so mighty and powerful, has vanished!

segs.p: Sace hi bhagavā ciraṁ dīghamaddhānaṁ tiṭṭheyya tadassa bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānan’ti.
segs.e: If the Buddha was to remain for a long time, that would be for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.’”

segs.p: Tathā hi panāyasmato sāriputtassa dīgharattaṁ ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā susamūhatā.
segs.e: “That must be because Venerable Sāriputta has long ago totally eradicated I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit.

segs.p: Tasmā āyasmato sāriputtassa satthupi vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā nuppajjeyyuṁ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti.
segs.e: So even if the Teacher were to decay and perish, it wouldn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress in him.”
Linked Discourses 21.3
1. Monks
A Mound of Salt
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā ca sāriputto āyasmā ca mahāmoggallāno rājagahe viharanti veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe ekavihāre.
segs.e: At that time the venerables Sāriputta and Moggallāna were staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā mahāmoggallāno tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā mahāmoggallānena saddhiṁ sammodi.
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Sāriputta came out of retreat, went to Venerable Moggallāna, and exchanged greetings with him.

segs.p: Sammodanīyaṁ kathaṁ sāraṇīyaṁ vītisāretvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṁ mahāmoggallānaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, Sāriputta sat down to one side, and said to Mahāmoggallāna:
“Reverend Moggallāna, your faculties are so very clear, and your complexion is pure and bright.

segs.p: parisuddho mukhavaṇṇo pariyodāto santena nūnāyasmā mahāmoggallāno ajja vihārena vihāsī”ti.
segs.e: Have you spent the day in a peaceful meditation?”
“Reverend, I’ve spent the day in a coarse meditation.

segs.p: Api ca me ahosi dhammī kathā”ti.
segs.e: But I have had some Dhamma talk.”

segs.p: “Kena saddhiṁ panāyasmato mahāmoggallānassa ahosi dhammī kathā”ti?
segs.e: “Who did you have a Dhamma talk with?”

segs.p: “Bhagavatā kho me, āvuso, saddhiṁ ahosi dhammī kathā”ti.
segs.e: “With the Buddha.”

segs.p: “Dūre kho, āvuso, bhagavā etarahi sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: “But Reverend, the Buddha is far away. He’s staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Kiṁ nu kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhagavantaṁ iddhiyā upasaṅkami;
segs.e: Did you go to him with your psychic power,

segs.p: udāhu bhagavā āyasmantaṁ mahāmoggallānaṁ iddhiyā upasaṅkamī”ti?
segs.e: or did he come to you?”
“No reverend, I didn’t go to him with my psychic power,
nor did he come to me.

segs.p: Api ca me yāvatā bhagavā ettāvatā dibbacakkhu visujjhi dibbā ca sotadhātu.
segs.e: Rather, the Buddha cleared his clairvoyance and clairaudience toward me,

segs.p: Bhagavatopi yāvatāhaṁ ettāvatā dibbacakkhu visujjhi dibbā ca sotadhātū”ti.
segs.e: and I cleared my clairvoyance and clairaudience toward him.”

segs.p: “Yathākathaṁ panāyasmato mahāmoggallānassa bhagavatā saddhiṁ ahosi dhammī kathā”ti?
segs.e: “But what manner of Dhamma talk did you have together?”
“Well, reverend, I said to the Buddha,
‘Sir, they speak of one who is energetic.

segs.p: Kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, āraddhavīriyo hotī’ti?
segs.e: How is an energetic person defined?’

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, maṁ, āvuso, bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: When I said this, the Buddha said,
‘Moggallāna, it’s when a mendicant lives with energy roused up:

segs.p: kāmaṁ taco ca nhāru ca aṭṭhi ca avasissatu, sarīre upassussatu maṁsalohitaṁ, yaṁ taṁ purisathāmena purisavīriyena purisaparakkamena pattabbaṁ na taṁ apāpuṇitvā vīriyassa saṇṭhānaṁ bhavissatīti.
segs.e: “Gladly, let only skin, sinews, and bones remain! Let the flesh and blood waste away in my body! I will not stop trying until I have achieved what is possible by human strength, energy, and vigor.”
That’s how an individual is energetic.’

segs.p: Evaṁ kho me, āvuso, bhagavatā saddhiṁ ahosi dhammī kathā”ti.
segs.e: That’s the Dhamma talk I had together with the Buddha.”

segs.p: “Seyyathāpi, āvuso, himavato pabbatarājassa parittā pāsāṇasakkharā yāvadeva upanikkhepanamattāya;
segs.e: “Reverend, next to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna I’m like a few pieces of gravel next to the Himalayas, the king of mountains.

segs.p: evameva kho mayaṁ āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa yāvadeva upanikkhepanamattāya.
Āyasmā hi mahāmoggallāno mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo ākaṅkhamāno kappaṁ tiṭṭheyyā”ti.
segs.e: Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is so mighty and powerful he could, if he wished, live on for the proper lifespan.”

segs.p: “Seyyathāpi, āvuso, mahatiyā loṇaghaṭāya parittā loṇasakkharāya yāvadeva upanikkhepanamattāya;
segs.e: “Reverend, next to Venerable Sāriputta I’m like a few grains of salt next to a mound of salt.

segs.p: evameva kho mayaṁ āyasmato sāriputtassa yāvadeva upanikkhepanamattāya.
Āyasmā hi sāriputto bhagavatā anekapariyāyena thomito vaṇṇito pasattho:
segs.e: Venerable Sāriputta has been commended, complimented, and praised by the Buddha:
‘Sāriputta is full of wisdom,
ethics, and peace.
Even a mendicant who has crossed over
might at best equal him.’”

segs.p: Itiha te ubho mahānāgā aññamaññassa subhāsitaṁ sulapitaṁ samanumodiṁsūti.
segs.e: And so these two spiritual giants agreed with each other’s fine words.
Linked Discourses 21.4
1. Monks
A Junior Mendicant
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena aññataro navo bhikkhu pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto vihāraṁ pavisitvā appossukko tuṇhībhūto saṅkasāyati, na bhikkhūnaṁ veyyāvaccaṁ karoti cīvarakārasamaye.
segs.e: Now at that time a certain junior monk, after his meal, on his return from almsround, entered his dwelling, where he adhered to passivity and silence. And he didn’t help the mendicants out when it was time to sew robes.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

segs.p: “idha, bhante, aññataro navo bhikkhu pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto vihāraṁ pavisitvā appossukko tuṇhībhūto saṅkasāyati, na bhikkhūnaṁ veyyāvaccaṁ karoti cīvarakārasamaye”ti.
Atha kho bhagavā aññataraṁ bhikkhuṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

segs.p: “ehi tvaṁ, bhikkhu, mama vacanena taṁ bhikkhuṁ āmantehi ‘satthā taṁ, āvuso, āmantetī’”ti.
segs.e: “Please, monk, in my name tell that monk that the Teacher summons him.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato paṭissutvā yena so bhikkhu tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā taṁ bhikkhuṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to that monk and said to him,
“Reverend, the Teacher summons you.”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho so bhikkhu tassa bhikkhuno paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho taṁ bhikkhuṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, reverend,” that monk replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

segs.p: “saccaṁ kira tvaṁ, bhikkhu, pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto vihāraṁ pavisitvā appossukko tuṇhībhūto saṅkasāyasi, na bhikkhūnaṁ veyyāvaccaṁ karosi cīvarakārasamaye”ti?
segs.e: “Is it really true, monk, that after your meal, on your return from almsround, you entered your dwelling, where you adhered to passivity and silence, and you didn’t help the mendicants out when it was time to sew robes?”
“Sir, I am doing my own work.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā tassa bhikkhuno cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya bhikkhū āmantesi:
segs.e: Then the Buddha, knowing that monk’s train of thought, addressed the mendicants:

segs.p: “mā kho tumhe, bhikkhave, etassa bhikkhuno ujjhāyittha.
segs.e: “Mendicants, don’t complain about this monk.

segs.p: Eso kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu catunnaṁ jhānānaṁ ābhicetasikānaṁ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṁ nikāmalābhī akicchalābhī akasiralābhī, yassa catthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajanti, tadanuttaraṁ brahmacariyapariyosānaṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī”ti.
segs.e: This monk gets the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when he wants, without trouble or difficulty. He has realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life, and lives having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“Not by being slack,
or with little strength
may this be realized—extinguishment,
the release from all suffering.
This young monk,
this best of men,
bears his final body,
having vanquished Māra with his legions.”
Linked Discourses 21.5
1. Monks
With Sujāta
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā sujāto yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami.
segs.e: Then Venerable Sujāta went to the Buddha.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ sujātaṁ dūratova āgacchantaṁ.
segs.e: The Buddha saw him coming off in the distance,
and addressed the mendicants:
“This gentleman shines in both ways.

segs.p: yañca abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgato, yassa catthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṁ brahmacariyapariyosānaṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī”ti.
segs.e: He’s attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty. And he has realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lives having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.”
That is what the Buddha said.
Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“This mendicant truly shines.
His heart is upright,
he’s unfettered, detached,
quenched by not grasping.
He bears his final body,
having vanquished Māra with his legions.”
Linked Discourses 21.6
1. Monks
With Bhaddiya the Dwarf
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā lakuṇḍakabhaddiyo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami.
segs.e: Then Venerable Bhaddiya the Dwarf went to the Buddha.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ lakuṇḍakabhaddiyaṁ dūratova āgacchantaṁ.
segs.e: The Buddha saw him coming off in the distance,
and addressed the mendicants:

segs.p: “passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, etaṁ bhikkhuṁ āgacchantaṁ dubbaṇṇaṁ duddasikaṁ okoṭimakaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ paribhūtarūpan”ti?
segs.e: “Mendicants, do you see this monk coming—ugly, unsightly, deformed, and despised by the mendicants?”
“Yes, sir.”

segs.p: “Eso kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo, na ca sā samāpatti sulabharūpā yā tena bhikkhunā asamāpannapubbā.
segs.e: “That mendicant is very mighty and powerful. It’s not easy to find an attainment that he has not already attained.

segs.p: Yassa catthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajanti, tadanuttaraṁ brahmacariyapariyosānaṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī”ti.
segs.e: And he has realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lives having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.”
That is what the Buddha said.
Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“Geese, herons, and peacocks,
elephants and spotted deer—
though their bodies are not equal,
they all fear the lion.
So it is for humans—
if a little person is wise,
they’re the truly great one,
not the fool with a good body.”
Linked Discourses 21.7
1. Monks
With Visākha, Pañcāli’s Son
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā vesāliyaṁ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṁ.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā visākho pañcālaputto upaṭṭhānasālāyaṁ bhikkhū dhammiyā kathāya sandasseti samādapeti samuttejeti sampahaṁseti, poriyā vācāya vissaṭṭhāya anelagalāya atthassa viññāpaniyā pariyāpannāya anissitāya.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Visākha, Pañcāli’s son, was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the mendicants in the assembly hall with a Dhamma talk. His words were polished, clear, articulate, expressing the meaning, comprehensive, and independent.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena upaṭṭhānasālā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi.
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the assembly hall. He sat down on the seat spread out,
and addressed the mendicants:

segs.p: “ko nu kho, bhikkhave, upaṭṭhānasālāyaṁ bhikkhū dhammiyā kathāya sandasseti samādapeti samuttejeti sampahaṁseti poriyā vācāya vissaṭṭhāya anelagalāya atthassa viññāpaniyā pariyāpannāya anissitāyā”ti?
segs.e: “Mendicants, who was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the mendicants in the assembly hall with a Dhamma talk?”

segs.p: “Āyasmā, bhante, visākho pañcālaputto upaṭṭhānasālāyaṁ bhikkhū dhammiyā kathāya sandasseti samādapeti samuttejeti sampahaṁseti, poriyā vācāya vissaṭṭhāya anelagalāya atthassa viññāpaniyā pariyāpannāya anissitāyā”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, it was Venerable Visākha, Pañcāli’s son.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ visākhaṁ pañcālaputtaṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: Then the Buddha said to Visākha:
“Good, good, Visākha!

segs.p: sādhu kho tvaṁ, visākha, bhikkhū dhammiyā kathāya sandassesi …pe… atthassa viññāpaniyā pariyāpannāya anissitāyā”ti.
segs.e: It’s good that you educate, encourage, fire up, and inspire the mendicants in the assembly hall with a Dhamma talk, with words that are polished, clear, articulate, expressing the meaning, comprehensive, and independent.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“Though an astute person is mixed up with fools,
they don’t know unless he speaks.
But when he speaks they know,
he’s teaching the state free of death.
He should speak and illustrate the teaching,
holding up the banner of the seers.
Words well spoken are the seers’ banner,
for the teaching is the banner of the seers.”
Linked Discourses 21.8
1. Monks
With Nanda
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā nando bhagavato mātucchāputto ākoṭitapaccākoṭitāni cīvarāni pārupitvā akkhīni añjetvā acchaṁ pattaṁ gahetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho āyasmantaṁ nandaṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Venerable Nanda—the Buddha’s cousin on his mother’s side—dressed in nicely pressed and ironed robes, applied eyeshadow, and took a glazed bowl. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

segs.p: “na kho te taṁ, nanda, patirūpaṁ kulaputtassa saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajitassa, yaṁ tvaṁ ākoṭitapaccākoṭitāni cīvarāni pārupeyyāsi, akkhīni ca añjeyyāsi, acchañca pattaṁ dhāreyyāsi.
segs.e: “Nanda, as a gentleman who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, it’s not appropriate for you to dress in nicely pressed and ironed robes, apply eyeshadow, and carry a glazed bowl.

segs.p: Etaṁ kho te, nanda, patirūpaṁ kulaputtassa saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajitassa, yaṁ tvaṁ āraññiko ca assasi, piṇḍapātiko ca paṁsukūliko ca kāmesu ca anapekkho vihareyyāsī”ti.
segs.e: It’s appropriate for you to stay in the wilderness, eat only almsfood, wear rag robes, and live without concern for sensual pleasures.”
That is what the Buddha said.
Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“When will I see Nanda
in the wilderness, wearing rag robes,
feeding on scraps offered by strangers,
unconcerned for sensual pleasures?”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā nando aparena samayena āraññiko ca piṇḍapātiko ca paṁsukūliko ca kāmesu ca anapekkho vihāsīti.
segs.e: Then some time later Venerable Nanda stayed in the wilderness, ate only almsfood, wore rag robes, and lived without concern for sensual pleasures.
Linked Discourses 21.9
1. Monks
With Tissa
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā tisso bhagavato pitucchāputto yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi dukkhī dummano assūni pavattayamāno. Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ tissaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Venerable Tissa—the Buddha’s cousin on his father’s side—went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. He was miserable and sad, with tears flowing. Then the Buddha said to him:

segs.p: “kiṁ nu kho tvaṁ, tissa, ekamantaṁ nisinno dukkhī dummano assūni pavattayamāno”ti?
segs.e: “Tissa, why are you sitting there so miserable and sad, with tears flowing?”

segs.p: “Tathā hi pana maṁ, bhante, bhikkhū samantā vācāyasannitodakena sañjambharimakaṁsū”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, it’s because the mendicants beset me on all sides with sneering and jeering.”

segs.p: “Tathāhi pana tvaṁ, tissa, vattā no ca vacanakkhamo;
segs.e: “That’s because you admonish others, but don’t accept admonition yourself.

segs.p: na kho te taṁ, tissa, patirūpaṁ kulaputtassa saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajitassa, yaṁ tvaṁ vattā no ca vacanakkhamo.
segs.e: As a gentleman who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, it’s not appropriate for you to admonish others without accepting admonition yourself.

segs.p: Etaṁ kho te, tissa, patirūpaṁ kulaputtassa saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajitassa:
segs.e: It’s appropriate for you to

segs.p: ‘yaṁ tvaṁ vattā ca assa vacanakkhamo cā’”ti.
segs.e: admonish others and accept admonition yourself.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“Why are you angry? Don’t be angry!
It’s better to not be angry, Tissa.
For this spiritual life is lived
in order to remove anger, conceit, and denigration.”
Linked Discourses 21.10
1. Monks
Senior In Name Only

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena aññataro bhikkhu theranāmako ekavihārī ceva hoti ekavihārassa ca vaṇṇavādī.
segs.e: Now at that time there was a certain mendicant who was Senior in name only. He lived alone and praised living alone.

segs.p: So eko gāmaṁ piṇḍāya pavisati eko paṭikkamati eko raho nisīdati eko caṅkamaṁ adhiṭṭhāti.
segs.e: He entered the village for alms alone, returned alone, sat in private alone, and focussed on walking mindfully alone.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

segs.p: “idha, bhante, aññataro bhikkhu theranāmako ekavihārī ekavihārassa ca vaṇṇavādī”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, there’s a certain mendicant who is Senior in name only. He lives alone and praises living alone.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā aññataraṁ bhikkhuṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

segs.p: “ehi tvaṁ, bhikkhu, mama vacanena theraṁ bhikkhuṁ āmantehi:
segs.e: “Please, monk, in my name tell the mendicant Senior that
the Teacher summons him.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato paṭissutvā yenāyasmā thero tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ theraṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to Venerable Senior and said to him,
“Reverend Senior, the Teacher summons you.”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā thero tassa bhikkhuno paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho āyasmantaṁ theraṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, reverend,” that monk replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

segs.p: “saccaṁ kira tvaṁ, thera, ekavihārī ekavihārassa ca vaṇṇavādī”ti?
segs.e: “Is it really true, Senior, that you live alone and praise living alone?”
“Yes, sir.”

segs.p: “Yathā kathaṁ pana tvaṁ, thera, ekavihārī ekavihārassa ca vaṇṇavādī”ti?
segs.e: “But in what way do you live alone and praise living alone?”

segs.p: “Idhāhaṁ, bhante, eko gāmaṁ piṇḍāya pavisāmi eko paṭikkamāmi eko raho nisīdāmi eko caṅkamaṁ adhiṭṭhāmi.
segs.e: “Well, sir, I enter the village for alms alone, return alone, sit in private alone, and focus on walking mindfully alone.

segs.p: Evaṁ khvāhaṁ, bhante, ekavihārī ekavihārassa ca vaṇṇavādī”ti.
segs.e: That’s how I live alone and praise living alone.”
“That is a kind of living alone, I don’t deny it.

segs.p: Api ca, thera, yathā ekavihāro vitthārena paripuṇṇo hoti
segs.e: But as to how living alone is fulfilled in detail,

segs.p: taṁ suṇāhi, sādhukaṁ manasi karohi; bhāsissāmī”ti.
segs.e: listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”
“Yes, sir,” he replied.
“And how, Senior, is living alone fulfilled in detail?

segs.p: Idha, thera, yaṁ atītaṁ taṁ pahīnaṁ, yaṁ anāgataṁ taṁ paṭinissaṭṭhaṁ, paccuppannesu ca attabhāvapaṭilābhesu chandarāgo suppaṭivinīto.
segs.e: It’s when what’s in the past is given up, what’s in the future is relinquished, and desire and greed for present incarnations is eliminated.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, thera, ekavihāro vitthārena paripuṇṇo hotī”ti.
segs.e: That’s how living alone is fulfilled in detail.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“The vanquisher of all, knower of all, so very intelligent,
is unsullied in the midst of all things.
He’s given up all, freed in the ending of craving:
I declare that man to be one who lives alone.”
Linked Discourses 21.11
1. Monks
With Mahākappina
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā mahākappino yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami.
segs.e: Then Venerable Mahākappina went to the Buddha.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ mahākappinaṁ dūratova āgacchantaṁ.
segs.e: The Buddha saw him coming off in the distance,
and addressed the mendicants:

segs.p: “passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, etaṁ bhikkhuṁ āgacchantaṁ odātakaṁ tanukaṁ tuṅganāsikan”ti?
segs.e: “Mendicants, do you see that monk coming—white, thin, with a pointy nose?”
“Yes, sir.”
“That mendicant is very mighty and powerful.

segs.p: Na ca sā samāpatti sulabharūpā yā tena bhikkhunā asamāpannapubbā.
segs.e: It’s not easy to find an attainment that he has not already attained.

segs.p: Yassa catthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṁ brahmacariyapariyosānaṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī”ti.
segs.e: And he has realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lives having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“The aristocrat is best among people
who take clan as the standard.
But one accomplished in knowledge and conduct
is best among gods and humans.
The sun blazes by day,
the moon radiates at night,
the aristocrat shines in armor,
and the brahmin shines in absorption.
But all day and all night,
the Buddha blazes with glory.”
Linked Discourses 21.12
1. Monks
Companions
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho dve bhikkhū sahāyakā āyasmato mahākappinassa saddhivihārino yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu.
segs.e: Then two mendicants who were companions, protégés of Venerable Mahākappina, went to the Buddha.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā te bhikkhū dūratova āgacchante.
segs.e: The Buddha saw them coming off in the distance,
and addressed the mendicants:

segs.p: “passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, ete bhikkhū sahāyake āgacchante kappinassa saddhivihārino”ti?
segs.e: “Mendicants, do you see those monks coming who are companions, protégés of Venerable Mahākappina?”
“Yes, sir.”
“Those mendicants are very mighty and powerful.

segs.p: Na ca sā samāpatti sulabharūpā, yā tehi bhikkhūhi asamāpannapubbā.
segs.e: It’s not easy to find an attainment that they have not already attained.

segs.p: Yassa catthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṁ brahmacariyapariyosānaṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti.
segs.e: And they’ve realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. They live having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“These companion mendicants
have been together for a long time.
The true teaching has brought them together,
the teaching proclaimed by the Buddha.
They’ve been well trained by Kappina
in the teaching proclaimed by the Noble One.
They bear their final body,
having vanquished Māra with his legions.”
The Linked Discourses on monks are complete.
The Book of Causality is finished.
